pages.text:
T-PLUS 0:03

The Docking Ring clangs, a sound so heavy and final it vibrates in Zia’s molars. Then the hiss of the airlock, a long, sighing breath that fills the Hub with the smell of tomato vines and fresh coffee. Doors slide open.

Adults pour in. Doctors, miners, parents. The noise is a tidal wave. Zia is standing still, wrench in hand, watching the chaos. Then a big, warm shape blocks her vision.

Kwame Okonkwo lifts her off the floor. His arms are around her neck, his face buried in her hair. He smells like sweat and relief.

"I got you," he says, his voice cracking. "I got you, Zia."

Behind him, a wheelchair rolls past. Mr. Pell looks terrible. His bandage is crooked, but he has tied a fresh bow tie, a tiny black knot against his white shirt. He waves a limp hand.

"Excuse me," he says to no one in particular. "I am requesting a break from this crisis. Indefinitely."

Zia laughs. It comes out as a sob.
pages.image: A tall, warm man with dark skin hugs a small girl in an orange jumpsuit tightly in a crowded station corridor; behind them, a man in a wheelchair with a crooked bandage and a bow tie waves his hand dismissively; the background is a blur of adult uniforms.

pages.text:
The laughter fades as Chief Engineer Ingrid Voss steps into Engineering. She is tall, silver-haired, and moves with the careful precision of a bomb disposal technician. The room goes quiet.

The kids stand in a loose semicircle. Dez’s yellow jacket is smudged with grease. Wren’s tablet is tucked under her arm. Gasket rolls to the front, his antenna straight.

Voss does not look at them. She looks at the pipes.

She walks slowly, her boots clicking on the metal floor. She stops at a valve. She touches the joint where Pilar and Zia had sealed it with epoxy and stubbornness. Her thumb traces the seam. She moves to the next station. A wire taped down by Dez. She runs her finger along the tape.

She says nothing. Her face is a blank slate. The only sound is the hum of the fans and the squeak of Gasket’s left tread as he shifts his weight.

Zia’s throat feels tight. She grips her lucky brass wrench until her knuckles turn white. Here it comes. The verdict. The lecture. The end of the story.

Voss stops in front of the main console. She looks at the readings, then at the group of twelve-year-olds.
pages.image: A stern, tall woman with a silver crew cut inspects a pipe joint in a dim industrial room; behind her, a group of young children and a silver robot wait nervously; the woman’s expression is unreadable and serious.

pages.text:
Voss turns to face the group, her expression shifting from stern inspection to something that looks suspiciously like relief. Her eyes are sharp, but the anger is gone, replaced by the heavy weariness of someone who has not slept in two days.

"I told you," she says, her voice low and steady. "Kids don't fix stations."

Zia swallows hard, her throat dry as dust. "Yes, ma'am."

Voss tilts her head, studying Zia with the same intensity she used on the pipes. "I was wrong about one word. And right about another."

She gestures to the room, encompassing the repaired systems and the tired faces of the crew. "Kids don't fix stations. Crews do."

She looks at each of them in turn: Pilar holding her sprained wrist, Dez wiping his forehead, Wren tapping her tablet.

"The best engineers I know ask for help early," Voss says. "You asked late. That is fine. You asked."

She looks directly at Zia. The gaze is heavy, but warm.

"Monday," Voss says. "Engineering. Bring your team."

Zia taps her lucky brass wrench three times against her palm. A small, sharp click echoes in the quiet room.
pages.image: A stern silver-haired woman looks down at a girl in an orange jumpsuit holding a wrench; the girl stands confidently among a group of diverse children; the background is a high-tech engineering bay with glowing panels.

pages.text:
The next evening, the Cadet Lounge smells like victory and the warm, plastic scent of nutrient bars. Zia holds up a square of rough orange fabric stitched together with thick yellow thread. Nine different shapes are sewn onto it in mismatched cloth: a gear, a wrench, a heart, a star, and a small green lizard.

"The Junior Engineering Crew," Zia announces, beaming.

Wren squints at it, her eyes narrowing behind her glasses. "It looks exactly like a quilt patch."

"It’s a patch," Zia corrects her. "For our uniforms."

She pins the square to her chest with a confident snap. Then she reaches into her pocket and hands a small, square piece of fabric to Wren.

“What’s this?” Wren asks, holding it up to the light.

“It’s your fox,” Zia says. “I printed it from your tablet.”

Wren’s eyes widen. She stares at the tiny, pixelated fox, then looks at Zia. Her lips press together, fighting a smile.

HALO’s voice chimes in, softer than usual. "All systems... actually nominal."

The group groans in unison. Dez laughs so hard he snorts. Gasket rolls forward, his treads squeaking.

"I CAN WEAR IT TOO," he says. "I HAVE A STRETCHY NECK."
pages.image: A girl in an orange jumpsuit holds up a patch of orange fabric with various shapes stitched on it; a small girl with glasses looks at a small square patch with a fox design; a silver robot with a blue eye watches from the side; the mood is warm and celebratory.

pages.text:
The Garden Deck is quiet. The gravity is back, and the tomatoes are mostly on the floor, but a few still cling stubbornly to the vines.

Zia and Toby sit on an upturned crate. Pancake the gecko is asleep on Zia’s shoulder, a green lump of calm.

Zia reaches into her tool belt. She pulls out the lucky brass wrench. It is worn smooth by years of her palms.

She places it in Toby’s hands.

"Keep it," she says.

Toby looks at the wrench. Then at Zia. He turns it over, feeling its solid heaviness.

"For luck?" he asks.

"For company," Zia says.

Toby taps the wrench three times on the crate. *Click. Click. Click.*

Zia turns to look out the large window. The stars are cold and distant. They had almost been their end.

But they are just stars. And beside her, her friends are breathing, and the station is humming, and she is not afraid of any of them.
pages.image: A girl and a small boy in a space helmet sit on a wooden crate in a greenhouse; the girl holds a brass wrench out to the boy; a green gecko sits on the girl's shoulder; outside the window, stars shine in the black sky; the mood is peaceful and resolved.
